alternatives.label: Crime, justice & behavioral evidence
alternatives.concept: Investigate crime and social responses through criminal-law reasoning, psychological and sociological explanation, developmental and cognitive evidence, and qualitative, quantitative and economic methods. Criminological research design, extremism prevention and inquiry into racialized crime and punishment anchor this broader composition. The comparison concerns the confirmed taught core; specialized victimology, Dutch policing and procedure, witness methods and cybercrime remain differences.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: Rational choice, game theory, costs and market foundations support economic explanations. Crime-control cost-benefit evaluation itself is not specified.
Choice under uncertainty, cognitive limitations, efficiency, externalities and government provide behavioural/economic tools. Not criminal-policy evaluation; BENGATE102 required.

Actual empirical design, measurement/sampling, survey construction, ethics, Ranalysis andperformed studentdata project supply introductory criminological-research methods and preparation for behavioural economics; no crime dataset promised.

Minority experience, emotion, identity safety and a substantive ethical survey project offer relevant behavioural/inequality methods. Leadership is not criminological intervention; BENGATE102 required.

Legal and sociolegal foundations include criminal, administrative, constitutional, tort and human-rights law, social control, race/gender, IRAC and mock trials. Strong partial foundation; broader than Dutch criminology law.
Human-rights inquiry includes torture, punishment and dignity. Concrete legal and normative complement, without full criminal procedure.

Criminal liability, criminalisation, punishment and a simulated legal clinic combine with an actual criminology or organised-crime research proposal. Strong subject response beyond a title match; not the complete policing, victimology or cybercrime curriculum.

Actual internationalcriminal/humanrights law, responsibility, force and refugee-protection case analysis add the policy direction’s public-law response to violence/communities; not Dutch criminalprocedure or ordinary policeorganization.
Administrative discretion, procedural fairness, remedies and judicial review support governance and legal-protection questions. Comparative rather than specifically Dutch criminal enforcement.
Utilitarian, deontological and other ethical arguments support moral and punishment reasoning. This is not empirical penology.
Moral and political emotions, fear, anger and decision-making deepen affective/social interpretation. Philosophical inquiry is not empirical forensic evidence.
Actual institutional comparison, democraticmeasurement, polarization, participation and empirical memo provide a concrete policy/institutional inquiry strand; not Dutch policing organization.
Description-only policy cycles, globalisation, a sugar case and policy memos receive full consideration. They support policy reasoning but do not establish criminal-policy cost-benefit analysis.

Actual structuralviolence, identity/colonialgrievances, counterterrorism/ruleoflaw, reconciliation and policybrief/dossier support the prevention/publicpolicy direction, with internationalconflict settings explicit.
Socialisation, groups, stratification, race/class and sociological case analysis support inequality and social explanations of crime. No claim that every case concerns crime.
Actual interviews, observation, document coding, ethics and team empirical research directly respond to the qualitative methods. Different software does not invalidate the academic relationship.
Functionalism, symbolic interactionism, stigma, critical theory and power support explanation and social construction of deviance. Not a full criminological-theory sequence.
Trust, solidarity, civil repair and public spheres provide specific institutional complements. Civil-society research is not automatically crime prevention.
Attention, memory, cognitive control, social cognition and experimental design provide concrete foundations for evidence and decision bias. A criminal-witness application is not guaranteed.
Learning, personality, social influence, neural mechanisms and mental disorders support psychological foundations. No unsupported claim about biological crime causation.
Aggression, prejudice, social cognition, group influence and empirical design support behavioural explanations. The project proposes a study rather than conducting one.
Substantial experimental design, ANOVA, multivariable analysis and R/SPSS work respond to quantitative research and experiments. Crime datasets are not required by this UCR course.

Actual forensic-psychology content, personality/substance disorders, stigma and biopsychosocial causation are meaningful connections. Do not equate mental illness with crime or claim complete forensic training.
Systematic reviews, meta-analysis, R, effects and bias strongly support evidence synthesis. A criminological application requires an actual supported focus; no original field experiment claimed.

Developmental risk and protection, adolescence, attachment and life-course analysis support offender-development questions. The actual interview involves an adult over50, not juvenile-offender fieldwork.

Actual radicalisation, violent extremism, terrorism, psychosocial risks/protection and educational prevention are direct subject connections. Research is translated into a toolkit and revised using recipient feedback.

Actual crime, punishment, the racialised body, incarceration, extremist propaganda and archival/observational methods offer concrete historical connections to criminalisation and communities. American focus; not Dutch procedure.

blocks: Both introduce legal sources, legal fields, law–society relations and legal reasoning. UCR is comparative and broader; Leiden applies the foundations specifically to criminologists and Dutch law.

Both teach criminal responsibility, legality, conditions for liability and punishment, using legal cases. Leiden also introduces Dutch criminal procedure and sanction law; UCR adds comparative doctrine, simulated legal aid and a criminological research proposal.

Both study public decision-making, administrative discretion, procedural fairness and legal remedies. UCR embeds this in comparative constitutional study; Leiden also teaches specific Dutch crime-control powers.

Both develop psychological and neurobiological explanations involving learning, personality, development and behaviour. Leiden applies them to offending; UCR supplies broader brain/behaviour foundations.

Both consider development and life-course explanations relevant to patterns of behaviour. UCR teaches developmental theory and life-story inquiry across the lifespan; Leiden centres offending, its consequences and experiences of detained people.

Both study attention and memory as foundations for understanding cognitive limitations. UCR investigates general cognitive functions and cognitive control, including an attentional-blink experiment; Leiden applies cognition to witnesses, recognition, interrogation, legal decisions and evidence valuation.
Both study social structures, socialization, groups, inequality and classical sociological explanation. Leiden consistently applies these theories to crime; UCR examines wider social phenomena.

Both compare explanatory theories and their assumptions in historical and social settings. UCR supplies functionalism, interactionism, stigma, critical and decolonial theory; it is not a dedicated sequence of criminological theories.

Both use choice, behaviour, efficiency and economic evaluation of intervention. UCR teaches broader microeconomic and behavioural models; Leiden additionally applies welfare economics and formal cost–benefit analysis to crime policy.

Both develop academic communication, source use, teamwork, reflection and societal engagement. Leiden frames these skills through criminological questions; UCR uses wider personal, academic and community work.

Both teach research design, measurement, quality criteria, ethical inquiry and empirical investigation. UCR includes statistical work and a student survey project; the topic is not guaranteed to be criminological.
Both teach interview, observation and qualitative fieldwork, ethical/reflexive analysis and reporting. The software and project settings differ.
Both develop multivariable quantitative analysis, R-based empirical reasoning, assumption checks and substantive reporting. UCR uses health/behavioural examples; Leiden uses criminological data.

Both use ethical theories and argued judgments to evaluate research and policy dilemmas. UCR provides a broader moral-philosophy course; Leiden also teaches philosophy of science and its application to criminological knowledge.
External study without a separately paired UCR course
Crime-related inquiry is distributed across the UCR composition; no separately allocated introductory Criminology survey is asserted.
The dedicated empirical/legal study of the Dutch criminal-justice chain has no separately paired UCR course.
No dedicated spatial and temporal analysis of offending, fear and victimization is supplied by the selected UCR courses. Environmental sustainability is not treated as environmental criminology.
The second criminological skills sequence is not a separate UCR counterpart. PPD is already paired with the first skill lab and is not counted twice.
Foundational statistics recur within broader UCR methods courses, but no additional separately allocated UCR course is paired here.
No selected course constitutes a dedicated victimology sequence. General psychology and life-story interviewing are not victim-support training.
UCR has broader qualitative, archival and visual inquiry, but no separately paired dedicated second criminological qualitative-analysis module.
Specific Dutch police/prosecutorial organization, strategies and decision practices remain distinct.
Cyber-offending, victimization, criminal digital environments and sanctions/interventions are not supplied by a general computing or AI-ethics course.
Experimental methods occur within broader UCR statistics/cognition courses, but no separately allocated dedicated criminological experiment-design course is paired here.
Genuine 30-EC choice space is retained without inventing a minor or fixed taught contents; approval, level and non-overlap conditions apply.

selection.assessment: Two sequentially supported whole UCR programmes respond to the confirmed core. The policy direction changes four substantive courses30EC, with current feasibility and meaningful institutional priorities. A third cyber-related fullschedule passes numerical constraints but fails the academic organizing-subject gate after actualtechnical/AIforensic content is credited. Stop at two; no quota or cosmeticthirdslot.

notes.text: The comparison assesses the confirmed 120-EC first-two-year academic core. The 30 EC of open study is shown without fixed contents; the remaining 30 EC of required third-year study, including the thesis and culmination, are excluded. Within the assessed core, Leiden retains specialized victimology, Dutch policing and procedure, witness-evidence methods, spatial criminology and cybercrime. UCR offers broader legal, behavioural, social and policy inquiry. Unpaired modules may share methods with broader UCR courses; they do not establish separate credit or specialist equivalence. Optional UCR research is additional to its scheduled 180 EC.

audience.programmeDescription: Criminology at Leiden studies crime, its causes and consequences, and the ways society responds to it. The programme combines legal, psychological and sociological perspectives with qualitative, quantitative and experimental research. Students examine offenders, victims, prevention, policing and criminal justice.
audience.comparisonExplanation: This qualified academic-core comparison assesses the confirmed first two years of Criminology through broader UCR legal, behavioral, social and policy study. It does not compare the complete Leiden degree or certify its progression. Specialized criminological subjects and practices remain differences within the assessed core.

curriculum.limitation: The displayed components total 150 EC: a confirmed 120-EC first-two-year academic core and 30 EC of open study. The remaining 30 EC of required third-year study, including the thesis, its detailed preparation and culmination, are excluded. The elective space has no fixed assumed contents, and full degree access is not certified. First-year tutoring and the Dutch criminological language test are zero-credit obligations.

componentNotes.y1-criminal-law: A compulsory first-year course. First-year Criminology students are registered for the programme’s courses by the university.
componentNotes.y2-quantitative-research-2: Builds on Quantitative Criminological Research 1; successful completion of that course is recommended before participation.
componentNotes.y2-qualitative-research-2: Develops qualitative analysis of secondary data and coding. The first-year research courses provide the preparatory foundation.
componentNotes.y3-open-electives: 30 EC of elective space. Choices must meet the applicable level, approval and non-overlap rules. Honours College courses do not count here; the Criminology minor cannot be used as a whole where it overlaps with compulsory study.
